newsitem.title: USA: POLL-US CPI growth seen edging up over next 2 yrs.
newsitem.headline: POLL-US CPI growth seen edging up over next 2 yrs.

text.p: U.S. consumer inflation is expected to rise moderately over the next two years, but a coinciding pickup in the jobless rate should help limit wage pressures and ward off sharp price hikes, said economists in the Reuters quarterly U.S. economic survey.

On average, economists projected that core Consumer Price Index (CPI) -- which excludes volatile food and energy components -- would rise gradually from an estimated 2.6-percent rate in the third quarter of 1997 to 3.2 percent in the first quarter of 1999.
Core CPI grew 2.6 percent in the year ended May 1997.

The experts also called for slow upticks in the unemployment rate after a third quarter in which unemployment remains steady at the second quarter's 4.9-percent average rate. The steady climb would then bring unemployment to an average rate of 5.4 percent in the second quarter of 1999.

The pundits largely agreed that any risk of higher inflation rested with the labor market. Some said Federal Reserve complacency had allowed wage pressures to build, clearing the path for higher inflation.

"There are pressures in the pipeline which eventually will show up and the Fed will have been too slow to keep them at bay," said Cynthia Latta, an economist at DRI/McGraw Hill. "We see inflation not really getting out of control, but (there is) some acceleration,"
But the central bank will take action eventually, and that should slow economic growth and limit the rise in inflation, Latta said.
"We still expect the Fed to raise interest rates ... (and) we do see some softening as a result of those Federal Reserve rate hikes," she said.
Mirroring the average forecasts, Latta projected two 25-basis-point increases in the key federal funds rate by the fourth quarter of this year.

A few experts projected a declining inflation rate. When asked how price increases could slow despite expectations of a continued low jobless rate, many cited global competition, improving producitivity and Fed vigilance.
"It's a matter of where you think the inflationary rate of unemployment is, and I think the answer is, nobody knows," said Suzanne Rizzo, a U.S. economist at MFR Inc.
Official interest rates and market rates would shoot up if price increases became more pronounced, and that would quickly stifle inflation, Rizzo said.
While the economists in the poll offered differing views on consumer prices, nearly all projected a sub-2.0-percent annual growth rate in the Producer Price Index (PPI) through 1998.
On average, the experts projected PPI would expand at an annual rate of 0.7 percent in 1997 and 1.7 percent in 1998.

Declines in the growth of food and energy prices beat the PPI into submission in recent months. Many economists said their forecasts simply represented a return of the index's growth to a more sustainable rate.
"I have the PPI picking up. It's a little on the weak side right now and it's got to come back," Rizzo said.
Explaining the gap between consumer and producer price growth, Kurt Karl, director of WEFA Group's U.S. forecasting center, said wage pressures weigh less heavily on PPI.
"The Producer Price Index is almost totally isolated from wage inflation," Karl said.
Contracts often limit the ability of suppliers to pass increased labor costs onto producer clients, he said.
